title: Definition of patch completeness — what's covered and what's not
body: Patch completeness in this plan means: 'the committed + staged surface is sufficient for the plan's tests to discover, the plan's imports to resolve, and CI to run on a fresh clone.' It does NOT cover: (a) environment variables / secrets needed at runtime — handled by environments.json + execution_env (F023 of orchestration plan); (b) external system state (Firebase rules, GCP IAM, etc.) — handled by per-feature acceptance evidence; (c) cross-file documentation completeness (e.g. updating README when a flag is added) — that's a code-audit concern, not a patch-completeness concern; (d) commit message accuracy — separate concern. Why: keep the gate narrow so it doesn't become a catch-all that grows past what it can mechanically verify. How to apply: when a future need to expand the gate appears, prefer adding it as a sibling check (e.g. doc-completeness gate, env-completeness gate) rather than overloading patch_completeness.

title: Operator override is plan-locked, not durable
body: Both override flags (`--allow-incomplete-patch <reason>` and `--unrelated-dirty-state-note <reason>`) are CLI flags supplied per dispatch invocation, NOT entries in a durable config file. Why: durable overrides drift into 'always set, never read' shape; per-dispatch overrides force the operator to think about WHY each time. The reason is also length-validated >=8 chars to make 'lazy bypass' patterns visible (a one-word reason like 'wip' won't pass). How to apply: future plans that consistently need an override should not add a config flag to silence the gate; instead they should fix the underlying surface (e.g. promote the file out of untracked, or add the file to the plan's evidence_refs).

title: Unrelated dirty state is detected heuristically, not authoritatively
body: The 'unrelated unstaged dirty state' rule uses a best-effort heuristic: implementer-touched = files cited in audit envelope's evidence_refs + files in plan's affected_paths (if present). Anything in unstaged_modified outside that set is treated as 'unrelated dirty state' and triggers the note requirement. Why: there is no authoritative way to know 'what files this plan should have touched' without operator input, and asking the operator to enumerate is heavier than asking them to acknowledge. The cost of false-positives (operator must add a note when files are actually in scope but not yet referenced) is judged lower than false-negatives (unrelated WIP slips through). How to apply: if false-positives become noisy, the right fix is to have implementers cite their touched files more thoroughly in evidence_refs — not to weaken the heuristic.

title: Schema promotion deferred to a separate conventions plan
body: F001 captures git_state as evidence sidecar (`evidence/git-state-<i>-<role>.json`); F003 records `patch_completeness` as an optional block in signoff.json validated locally but NOT in the v1.0 schema. Why: bumping `audit.schema.json` to v1.4.0 to add `git_state` AND bumping `signoff.schema.json` for the override block is a conventions-bump multi-step (agent-conventions repo bump + Pydantic update + subtree pull, mirrors F023 EC1's pattern), which would triple this plan's surface and lock the shape before we've used it. How to apply: after this plan ships and we have ~2-3 plans of lived experience with the field shapes, open `feat-patch-completeness-schema-promote` to bump v1.4.0 and migrate evidence sidecars into the canonical envelope. Until then: the sidecar shape is allowed to evolve.

title: Python-only import detection from touched-set files only; cross-language deferred
body: F002 detects imports via Python's `ast` module from the **touched-set** of files only — `touched_files ∪ staged ∪ unstaged_modified`. The full repo is NOT walked. Bash sourcing (`. ./helper.sh`), YAML workflow `uses:` lines pointing at local scripts, markdown links to in-repo files, and TOML `[tool.X.script]` references are NOT detected. Why: (a) shipping Python-only first lets us validate the gate's value without a multi-language detector burden; (b) bounding the read surface to the touched-set keeps the analyzer fast and avoids surfacing pre-existing repo-wide hygiene issues that aren't this plan's concern — patch-completeness checks the patch, not the whole tree. How to apply: bash/yaml detection lands as a follow-up only when a real plan trips on a missed cross-language reference. If a future need to analyze beyond the touched-set surfaces, prefer adding a sibling check (e.g. repo-wide hygiene gate) rather than widening this one.

title: Generated-artifact deny-list is conservative, project-specific extensions deferred
body: F002 ships a starter deny-list: `__pycache__/`, `*.pyc`, `*.pyo`, `.coverage`, `.DS_Store`, `.pytest_cache/`, `node_modules/`, `.tox/`, `.mypy_cache/`, `.ruff_cache/`. Each pattern carries a code-comment citation (mirrors F001 of the security baseline plan). Project-specific build outputs (e.g. `dist/`, `build/`, `target/`, language-server caches, IDE folders) are NOT included. Why: an aggressive deny-list will false-positive on plans that legitimately stage a one-off build artifact for evidence. How to apply: project-specific deny-list extensions land via per-plan operator config in a later plan if the need surfaces; the starter list covers the universal Python+macOS cases.

title: Plan does not bundle EC5 platform fix or delivery-profile work
body: Earlier scoping discussion considered bundling target-context (EC5) platform-fix and a delivery-profile classifier into one 'platform hardening' plan. Rejected: (a) EC5 fix touches prompt rendering + audit envelope formatting — a different surface; (b) delivery-profile classifier is a much larger schema-and-supervisor change that should consume patch-completeness as one of its mandatory phases, not co-design with it. Why: each of those plans has its own review needs (EC5 = audit-envelope shape, classifier = schema lock); bundling would create a 'too big to land' slice. How to apply: future platform-hardening plans should justify their slicing in their own plan.md scope section; do NOT retroactively absorb work that's already shipping in a sibling plan.

title: Analyzer output envelope shape — forward-compat with future schema promotion
body: F002's `check()` returns `CompletenessReport(status, findings, files)` where each `Finding = (mode, files, reason, severity, recommendation)`. NOT a flat `list[Finding]`. Why: when D004's follow-up plan promotes patch-completeness to `audit.schema.json` v1.4.0, the schema needs a stable envelope with overall status + per-finding severity + operator-actionable recommendation — these can't be retrofitted later without breaking the validator. By baking the envelope into v1 of the in-tree dataclass, schema promotion becomes a paste-in operation rather than a re-design. How to apply: any future addition (new mode, new severity tier, additional metadata) goes ONTO the existing envelope (extend Finding, add fields to CompletenessReport) — do not create a parallel return type. The JSON round-trip test in F002 pins the shape so accidental drift is caught.

title: Failure severity carve-out — gate fires at signoff/commit-readiness, not dry-run
body: The patch-completeness gate runs during `--strict-dry-run` and persists its report, but does NOT exit non-zero in dry-run mode. The hard block fires only when the supervisor would otherwise flip `passes:true` and write signoff. Why: dry-run is the operator's preview surface — it must surface findings (otherwise the operator can't fix them before committing) without aborting the dry-run flow (otherwise the operator can't see other gate states downstream). Conflating dry-run with commit-readiness would force operators to run with override flags during normal preview, defeating the gate. How to apply: any future gate added to the supervisor's pre-signoff hook must follow the same pattern — dry-run surfaces findings, signoff/commit-readiness blocks. Tests must exercise both paths.

title: Recovery framing corrected — pre_merge is upfront, not sequential
body: Earlier recovery proposal was 're-arm pre_merge to restore post-implementation review.' Discovered during dogfood of plan 2026-05-02-001 that the supervisor evaluates ALL declared human_gates BEFORE the implementer runs (gates-evaluated-upfront pattern, also in feedback_orchestrator_dogfood_lessons memory). Re-arming pre_merge would only add another upfront pause, NOT restore post-impl review. Honest recovery options for plan 004's currently-cleared gate state: (a) accept the cleared state and document this D-entry as the audit reason — operator reviews findings post-volley via gate-state-history + INBOX + audit envelopes, same as every prior signed-off plan; OR (b) re-arm pre_merge knowing it functions as a second upfront 'are you sure' rather than a finding-review checkpoint. Both produce equivalent post-volley review semantics. Why: documenting the platform truth in audit history prevents future operators from reaching for protection that doesn't currently exist. How to apply: see plan 2026-05-02-001 D005 for the full platform-semantics note + queued (not opened) follow-up plan for phase-aware gates.
